issues.issue: This clause fixes the integrated documents as "Parts I-VI ... as well as the Rate Sheet(s), Personal Fee Schedule(s) and Account Maintenance Information grid(s)", but Part VI's "Entire Agreement; Conflict Of Terms" clause declares the Night Depository Agreement to be the entire agreement on that service and to control over the Deposit Account Agreement. Which document integrates which, and whether items such as the "Important Information for Consumers about your TD Bank Checking Account" brochure referenced in the Overdrafts section are part of the contract, cannot be settled from this clause alone.

"Account" is defined here as only Checking, Money Market, personal CD and/or Savings Accounts, while Part II §1 (Accounts Covered) sweeps in "ALL personal deposit Accounts" including Passbook Savings, and other provisions govern Health Savings, Holiday Club and Club Saver Accounts. Whether obligations framed in terms of "Account" reach those other account types is unresolvable from this definition.

"Business Day" is defined as every day except Saturdays, Sundays and federal holidays, but the Funds Availability Policy repeatedly qualifies it as "a Business Day that we are open" and "the next Business Day we are open", implying Business Days on which the Bank is not open. The two usages cannot both be given the defined meaning.

"You" is defined as each depositor and any joint owner, but Part VI (Night Depository Agreement) separately provides that "you" and "your" refer to "the Depositor", and other provisions address custodians, trustees and Authorized Signers who are not depositors or joint owners. Which persons are bound by obligations addressed to "you" is therefore contestable.

The clause makes the Agreement control wherever its provisions "vary from" the UCC as adopted where the Account was opened, without identifying which UCC provisions are variable; UCC Article 4 makes some duties (good faith, ordinary care) non-disclaimable. The word "vary" and the unlimited scope of the override are what a court would have to construe.

"Any additional reasonable charges we may impose for services you request which are not contemplated by this Agreement" leaves "reasonable" undefined and gives no benchmark, while simultaneously allowing the Fee Schedule to be "amended from time to time". Whether a given charge is "reasonable" or was "requested" is left open.

The prohibition extends to restricted transactions processed through "your Account or any relationship between you and the Bank", a phrase with no stated boundary. What counts as a "relationship" outside the Account is undefined.

The consent is triggered only "if you give a cell phone number directly to us", leaving unresolved whether numbers supplied to agents, on applications, or later acquired are covered, and it is open-ended as to duration and revocability. "Directly to us" is the term a court would construe.

The clause makes the "form of ownership specified on the signature card" decisive and says "only the portion corresponding" applies, but supplies no rule where the card is silent, ambiguous, or inconsistent with how the Account is titled. The trigger term "specified" carries the whole allocation of ownership rights.

The clause conclusively imputes an intent to create survivorship rights from the mere act of signing a signature card as co-owner ("Each of you intends that ..."), a deemed intention that may not match the depositors' actual intent or state ownership law. Whether signing alone establishes survivorship is the construction question.

"All deposits are the property of all of the owners of the Account" states an ownership rule as between the co-owners without qualification, though the same joint-account rules elsewhere treat the balance as belonging to the survivor and subject to set-off for one owner's debts. Whether this sentence governs beneficial ownership or only the Bank's dealings is unclear.

Within the same paragraph, "None of you may instruct us to take away any of the rights of another" sits against the following sentence permitting any single owner to give "written notice ... not to pay any joint deposit", after which the Bank may refuse all payments. The two sentences cannot both be applied to a one-owner freeze instruction.

The clause turns on "any Authorized Signer", a capitalized term that is never defined anywhere in the Agreement's Definitions or elsewhere. Who qualifies as an Authorized Signer, as opposed to an owner or a person merely listed on a signature card, is left open.

The clause provides for the Account to pass to the named beneficiary "if that person is still living" but says nothing about who takes if the beneficiary predeceases the trustee or if several beneficiaries are named. That gap, plus the deemed characterization as a "Revocable Unwritten Trust", is what would be construed.

This clause limits changes and withdrawals for "either of these Trust Account types" to what is "permitted by the trust instrument or court order", but the Unwritten Trust described in the immediately preceding clause exists precisely where no written trust instrument or court order was provided. Read together with that clause, the limitation has nothing to operate on, and it also contradicts the statement there that the trustee "may withdraw all of the funds during your lifetime".

The bracketed passage leaves the age of the "minor" to vary between eighteen and twenty-one "depending on the jurisdiction ... and the circumstances", and the transfer duty is triggered at majority "or at another time determined by applicable law". When the custodianship ends, and thus when the Bank must transfer the funds, is not fixed by the text.

The Bank's discretion to "delay or refuse to give you provisional credit" and its power to "determine when final credit is received" sit against Part III's Funds Availability Policy, which commits the Bank to fixed availability schedules for deposited items. Which controls when the Bank withholds provisional credit on an item that the Policy makes available is not resolved.

This clause states flatly that "The Funds Availability Policy does not apply to items we have accepted for collection only", but Part III's "Non-U.S. Financial Institutions" section, itself part of that Policy, prescribes availability for items sent for collection (generally within thirty Calendar Days, and by the third Business Day for Canadian items not sent for collection). The two cannot both be given effect for foreign collection items.

The clause manufactures a waiver of the customer's "right to receive immediate notice of dishonor" from the Bank's mere option to re-present the item ("This means that you are waiving"), without any separate assent or notice mechanism. Whether re-presentment effects that waiver is the construction question.

"Typically, the Bank will cash checks drawn on other banks for its customers who have adequate available funds" is hedged by "typically" and by the undefined standard of "adequate available funds", so it is unclear whether any obligation to cash is created at all. The word "typically" is what a court would have to construe.

This clause reserves a seven Calendar Day notice right for all Savings and Money Market Accounts, while the sub-account provision reserving the same seven-day right adds that "the Bank does not presently exercise this right". Whether the Bank may in fact impose the notice requirement on savings withdrawals turns on reading the two reservations together.

"Repeated violations will result in the Account being closed or changed from a savings type Account to a transaction Account" gives no number, period or standard for "repeated". The trigger for the mandatory consequence is therefore indeterminate.

This clause measures excess withdrawals "in any calendar month", whereas the immediately preceding savings-withdrawal clause measures them by "any monthly period (based on your statement date)". Which period governs a Holiday Club or Club Saver Account whose statement cycle is not a calendar month is unresolved.

The clause assures that sub-account transfers cause "no adverse impact on the availability of the balances held in your Checking Account", yet the same paragraph caps transfers out of the non-transaction sub-account at six per statement cycle and gives the Bank unfettered discretion over the transfer threshold. The assurance and the limitation pull against each other.

The clause reserves a seven Calendar Day notice right and then says "the Bank does not presently exercise this right", leaving open whether and with what notice the Bank could begin to exercise it. "Does not presently exercise" is the phrase requiring construction.

After five specific withholding triggers, item (f) adds "there may be other reasons why we may be required to do so under applicable law", a catch-all that swallows the enumerated list. Whether the list is exhaustive or merely illustrative is the classic construction question.

Reporting to consumer reporting agencies is triggered where an Account "is closed for insufficient funds activity or other negative reason", and "other negative reason" has no stated limit against the single specific it follows. The scope of the reportable closures is left open.

This clause excuses the Bank from sending a statement in three situations, yet the limitation-on-claims clause runs the customer's fourteen- and thirty-day reporting periods from the date "we mailed a statement (or otherwise made it available to you)". How the reporting deadlines operate when no statement is sent at all cannot be answered from either clause alone.

This clause states the review-and-report duty in open terms ("promptly", "as soon as possible", "call us at once"), while the later clause fixes fourteen Calendar Days as reasonable and thirty Calendar Days as an absolute bar. Whether the flexible standard here or the fixed periods there measure the customer's duty is a genuine question.

The clause deems statements and check images "available" as of the statement mailing date irrespective of receipt, which is the event that starts every reporting period. Whether "available" can be deemed to occur on mailing, particularly where the Bank never mails or the customer never receives, is what would be construed.

Failure or refusal to do "these things" — cooperate, seek criminal and civil penalties, file reports and complaints, and give a sworn statement — is deemed a ratification of the defect in the item. The scope of the required "cooperation" and the deemed ratification consequence are both open to construction.

The clause sets two different periods for the same conduct: fourteen Calendar Days is agreed to be "a reasonable amount of time ... to review your Account statement and report any errors", but claims are barred only if not reported within thirty Calendar Days. Which period governs a customer who reports on day twenty is not stated.

The thirty Calendar Day bar covers "any error, forgery or other problem relating to a matter shown on an Account statement", while Part IV's Unauthorized Transfers section gives the customer sixty Calendar Days after the statement was mailed to report transfers he did not make. The two notice deadlines cannot both govern an unauthorized electronic debit appearing on a statement.

The Bank may destroy original checks "not less than thirty (30) Calendar Days after the statement mailing date", which is the same day the customer's thirty-Calendar-Day window to report a forgery under the preceding clause expires. Destruction of the evidence at the very moment the claim must be asserted is a tension between the two clauses.

The Bank may refuse a check that is not "in a form supplied by or previously approved by the Bank" or which is "incompletely or defectively drawn", with no standard for approval and no definition of defective drawing. Both phrases leave the refusal right without an ascertainable boundary.

The definition of "item" closes a long enumerated list with "any other instruction or order for the payment, transfer or withdrawal of funds", a catch-all that governs which transactions are subject to the posting order and to overdraft fees. Whether the general words are limited by the enumerated specifics is the construction question.

The whole posting mechanism turns on "your available Account balance", a phrase never defined and used differently across subparagraphs (a) adds available deposits, (b) subtracts unpaid pending authorizations. Whether "available balance" means the ledger balance, the Funds Availability Policy balance, or that balance net of pending holds is exactly what a fee dispute would turn on.

The Bank deducts pending authorizations from the available balance "subject to certain exceptions", and the exceptions are then said to include an open-ended set of "certain merchants that frequently request authorization for amounts in excess of the likely transaction amount". Neither the exceptions nor the merchant category is fixed, so the customer cannot determine his available balance.

The category scheme leaves it uncertain which fees fall in category (ii), (iii) or (iv), and "within categories i, ii, and iii, we post items in order from largest to smallest" does not say whether items presented on the same day in different categories are ordered by category or by size. The high-to-low rule and the category boundaries are the terms in dispute.

Overdraft fees "may be assessed on items presented for payment that bring your Account into a negative balance", but "negative balance" is not defined and the same paragraph distinguishes the available balance (reduced by pending authorizations) from the balance on which fees are charged. Whether a fee is owed turns on which balance the phrase means and on the permissive "may".

The Bank promises "advance notice" before changing its processing order but fixes no period, form or method for that notice. What notice suffices, and whether it must satisfy the separate Amendments clause, is left open by the phrase "advance notice".

The enumerated grounds for refusing an item end with "(e) we believe is otherwise not properly payable", a general catch-all sitting against the specific grounds that precede it. Whether "otherwise not properly payable" is confined to defects of the enumerated kind is the construction question.

The clause gives two examples of restrictive legends and then extends to legends "and the like", without any criterion for what other notations count as restrictive legends the Bank may disregard. The catch-all is the term needing construction.

The clause has the customer agree in advance never to postdate and denies him any remedy if an early-presented postdated check is paid, without any notice mechanism of the kind postdating rules ordinarily require. Whether that blanket advance waiver of "any loss to you" is effective is what would be construed.

The clause deems any debit initiated by a party to whom the customer voluntarily gave Account information "authorized by you", while Part IV's Unauthorized Transfers section and Electronic Check Conversions provisions give the customer rights over transfers made "using information from your check" without permission. The two treatments of the same debit cannot both stand.

An overdraft is defined here as an advance of funds greater than the amount "that has become available in accordance with the Bank's Funds Availability Policy", whereas the Processing Order clauses measure overdrafts against an "available Account balance" that is further reduced by pending debit-card authorizations. Which measure determines whether an overdraft — and hence a fee — has occurred cannot be answered from either provision alone.

This clause says a fee is charged "for each transaction that overdraws your account" only if the "negative available balance exceeds $5 at the end of the day", while the Processing Order clause states that overdraft fees may be assessed on any item that brings the Account into a negative balance and on every subsequent item while it stays negative. The two rules for when a fee is earned cannot both be applied to the same day's items.

This clause obliges the customer to pay "all of our costs of collecting an overdraft ... includ[ing] ... our legal fees and expenses", whereas the "If You Owe Us Money" clause limits recovery to "court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees as awarded by the court". Which measure of fees applies to a suit to collect an overdraft is unresolved between them.

The clause repeats three times that the fee may be charged when the Account "remains in overdrawn status for ten (10) consecutive Business Days" without saying whether the fee is charged once or recurs for each further ten-day period, and "overdrawn status" is not defined. Whether a second or third sustained fee is authorized is left open.

Closure is triggered either at sixty Calendar Days or at "such earlier time that we determine that the overdraft balance is uncollectible", a determination committed entirely to the Bank with no standard. The uncollectibility trigger is what a court would have to construe.

A stop payment request is effective only if it "precisely identif[ies] the Account number, check number, date and amount of the item, and the payee", a strict-accuracy requirement with no tolerance for an immaterial error. Whether "precisely" defeats a request describing the item with substantial accuracy is the construction question.

The clause makes an oral stop payment effective for a full year "[r]egardless of whether" it was made orally or in writing, but then requires written requests to be on a Bank-supplied form and makes the customer responsible for the accuracy of the written confirmation. Whether an oral request survives an inaccurate or unreturned confirmation is not answered.

The clause both says "reasonable time depends on the circumstances" and fixes a safe harbour ending the next Business Day, leaving unclear whether the safe harbour is the only measure or merely one sufficient case. "Reasonable time" is the term carrying the Bank's whole exposure for paying over a stop order.

This clause promises payment of the customer's established loss "up to the face amount of the check" for payment over a stop order, but the Limited Liability clause caps all recovery at the total fees paid in the preceding three months and bars liability absent bad faith. The two limits on the same claim cannot both control.

The Bank will attempt a stop only if the customer "certif[ies] to our satisfaction" that the item was lost, stolen or destroyed, a wholly subjective trigger, and "other similar item" is undefined alongside cashier's and teller's checks. Both phrases leave the Bank's duty indeterminate.

New fee rules "will take effect after the Change Date" while the parallel interest rule takes effect "on the day" of the change, so it is unclear whether fees assessed on the Change Date itself, or cycle-end fees for a period spanning the change, follow the old or new rules. "After the Change Date" is the phrase to construe.

The first sentence limits recognition of an attorney-in-fact to the period before written or actual notice of revocation, but the last sentence disclaims liability for "any payment made to, or at the direction of, a person holding a power of attorney" without that limit. Whether the disclaimer covers payments after notice of revocation is left open.

"We need not honor any claim against or involving an Account" absent a court order is then applied to "any person asserting any rights or interest regarding an Account, including you", which on its face lets the Bank refuse the depositor's own demand for his funds. The word "claim" and the inclusion of the depositor are what would be construed.

Suspension may follow any claim, dispute or proceeding the Bank "reasonably believe[s] involves you", on "any Account which we believe to be affected", and is expressly permitted even when due to "inadvertence, error because of similarity of the names of depositors, or other mistake". The belief-based trigger has no ascertainable limit and no stated duration.

The Bank may comply with any legal process "which we believe to be valid, without any liability from us to you", making the Bank's own belief the measure of a customer's rights against it. Whether that belief must be reasonable or in good faith is not stated.

The Bank is "entitled to a processing fee" on receipt of legal process without any amount, cap or cross-reference, while the Agreement elsewhere promises that charges are those "listed on the Personal Fee Schedule and Account Maintenance Information grid". What the customer has agreed to pay cannot be determined from the two read together.

The customer agrees the Bank may comply with legal process "irrespective of how and/or where it was received even if the law requires any particular method of service", an advance agreement to disregard statutory service requirements. Whether a depositor can contract away the service protections of process directed at his funds is the question.

This clause requires indemnity for legal actions "including any interpleader action we commence involving you or your Account", yet the general Indemnity clause states that "[t]his indemnification does not apply to claims that you may assert against us". Whether the customer must indemnify the Bank in litigation the Bank brings against him cannot be settled from either clause alone.

"Upon initiation of an interpleader action, we will be relieved and discharged of all further duties and obligations" does not say whether the discharge is confined to the disputed funds or extends to every duty the Bank owes under the Agreement. The scope of "all further duties and obligations" is the defect.

Recovery here is limited to "court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees as awarded by the court and as permitted by law", while the Overdrafts clause makes the customer liable for "all of our costs of collecting an overdraft ... to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law", including legal fees. Which applies to a suit over an overdraft is unresolved.

Set-off is available for "any debt you owe us that is in default", but the Agreement's Default clause defines default only in terms of the Account and includes triggers resting on the Bank's "sole discretion" as to your "condition or affairs". Whether a debt is "in default" for set-off purposes therefore depends on a clause written for a different purpose.

A hold may be placed whenever the Bank "ha[s] a claim against you or pending exercise of our right of set-off", with no stated duration, notice or release condition. The open-ended hold power is what a court would have to construe.

The security interest is granted in "your deposit Accounts" without any of the carve-outs the immediately preceding Right of Set-Off clause makes for IRAs, Health Savings and Coverdell Accounts and for consumer credit card debt. Whether the security interest can reach accounts the set-off right cannot is a direct tension between the two.

The duty to return items runs to "[c]ertain checks or other items made payable to a deceased joint Account holder", identified only by the parenthetical example of Social Security checks or electronic deposits. Which items are "certain" ones that must be returned is not ascertainable from the text.

This clause bars liability "unless we have acted in bad faith" and caps any recovery at three months' fees, while Part IV's "Our Liability" clause states that if the Bank fails to complete a transfer on time or in the correct amount "we will be liable for losses or damages" subject only to its own enumerated exceptions, and Part VI imposes a negligence standard. The three liability regimes cannot all govern the same loss.

"Bad faith" is used as the sole threshold for any liability but is nowhere defined, and it sits against the Agreement's own carve-out "unless expressly prohibited or otherwise restricted by applicable law, this Agreement, or the Electronic Funds Transfers Disclosure". What conduct amounts to bad faith, and whether ordinary-care failures are covered, is left open.

The disclaimer that the relationship is only "debtor and creditor" and creates no "fiduciary, quasi-fiduciary, or special relationship" sits against the Trust Account, UTMA and fiduciary-account provisions under which the Bank administers accounts held for beneficiaries and minors. How the disclaimer operates on those accounts requires reading the two together.

Default includes "(g) we, in our sole discretion, are not satisfied with your condition or affairs, financial or otherwise" and "(h) we, in our sole discretion, believe that your financial condition has suffered an adverse change", neither of which has any objective content. These sole-discretion triggers make the enumerated grounds that precede them superfluous.

The indemnity covers third-party claims arising out of action "taken or omitted to be taken by ... (ii) us in reliance upon any certification, evidence of authority, or other document", i.e. the Bank's own conduct, while the last sentence carves out only "claims that you may assert against us". How far the customer indemnifies the Bank for the Bank's own acts is the construction question.

This indemnity for following the customer's instructions is not limited to third-party claims, unlike the general Indemnity clause immediately above it, which is confined to claims "asserted against us by any third party" and expressly excludes claims the customer asserts. Whether this paragraph indemnifies the Bank against the customer's own claims turns on reading the two subparagraphs together.

The declaration that "THE PROVISIONS OF THIS SECTION SHALL BE SUBJECT TO NO EXCEPTIONS" cannot be squared with the Severability clause, which contemplates that any invalid provision will be reformed or treated as not written. Whether the jury waiver survives, or is reformed, in a jurisdiction that will not enforce pre-dispute waivers is the resulting question.

The right to close "any Account at any time, and for any reason, or no reason" makes the carefully enumerated grounds in the Default clause, and the remedy of closure it authorises, entirely superfluous. Whether closure is unconstrained or must rest on a default is the question the two raise together.

The authorization to deduct a returned direct deposit "from this Account or any other Account you may have with us" carries none of the exclusions the Right of Set-Off clause makes for IRAs, Health Savings and Coverdell Accounts. Whether this self-help deduction may reach protected accounts is unresolved between the two clauses.

"We may consider any Account ... having a zero balance for forty-five (45) Calendar Days to be closed by you" deems a closure by the customer without notice and without saying when or whether the Account can be reinstated. The deemed-closure mechanism and its effect on the surviving obligations are what a court would construe.

"Any communication we send to you at the last address as shown on our records will be binding on you for all purposes", even though the Bank may itself change that address on Postal Service information "without notice to you". The clause binds the customer to notices sent to an address he never supplied.

The Account is made subject to "our usual banking practices" and to "the general commercial banking practices in the area we serve", neither of which is defined or published anywhere in the Agreement. What those practices are, and how they rank against the Bank's internal policies which another clause says impose no standard of care, is left entirely open.

The clause requires an invalid provision to be "reformed in order to preserve the original intent of this Agreement to the fullest extent feasible", with no standard for feasibility or for who performs the reformation. "Feasible" is the term that decides whether the provision is rewritten or struck.

Governing law is fixed by "the jurisdiction in which the Store where you opened your Account is located", but "Store" is defined as a branch office and the Agreement elsewhere contemplates Accounts opened and maintained without one, and Part VI instead applies "the state laws that apply to your primary deposit account". Which state's law governs a given Account is therefore not determinable from the clause.

The Bank may change any term "at any time" and will give "such notice of the change as we determine is appropriate", with the customer's "continued use of the Account" deemed consent. The notice obligation is measured only by the Bank's own judgment, which is what a court would be asked to construe.

This clause lets the Bank set its own notice for changes to "the terms of this Agreement", while Part II §7 (Fees & Charges) promises "You will be notified at least thirty (30) days in advance of any changes to these fees". For a fee change the two notice rules cannot both govern.

"Accounts" is defined here to include "ALL personal deposit Accounts" including Passbook Savings and CDs, whereas the Agreement's Definitions section limits "Account" to Checking, Money Market, personal CD and Savings Accounts "unless limited by the heading under which it appears". The same defined term carries two different scopes in the one instrument.

The Rate Sheet is made "part of this disclosure" and thus of the Agreement, yet the following clause provides that rates "are subject to change at any time without notice" and the Amendments clause requires notice of changes to Agreement terms. Whether a rate change is an amendment requiring notice cannot be answered from this clause alone.

The note refers to rates "accurate as of the date shown on our Retail Rate Sheet" and to "the toll-free number listed on the back of this disclosure", neither of which matches the "Rate Sheet" incorporated by the preceding clause or anything printed in the document. The cross-references do not resolve to identifiable documents.

"Savings Transaction Accounts" appears only here and is not among the account types defined or described anywhere else in the Agreement. Which product this non-interest-bearing category covers cannot be determined from the text.

Rates are "adjusted periodically by the Bank based on various economic factors" with "no limit on changes up or down" and no notice, giving no ascertainable standard or frequency. "Various economic factors" is the phrase carrying the entire pricing discretion.

This clause conditions the disclosed APY on maintaining "the minimum tier balance in the Account each day", while the balance-tier clauses (2A–2E) state that the rate for the appropriate tier "will be paid on the full balance in the Account". Whether a single day below the tier minimum forfeits the tier rate is unresolved between them.

The text says "[a]n eligible account is a personal TD Bank Checking, Mortgage, Home Equity, or Credit Card account", but the table beneath it lists Home Equity Line of Credit and Home Equity Loan separately and adds a transaction requirement for Checking accounts that the sentence omits. The narrative and the table state different eligibility rules.

This clause treats the account as qualifying if there is "a linked, eligible personal Account (Checking, Mortgage, Home Equity Loan, Home Equity Line of Credit or Credit Card Account)", dropping the requirement in the preceding eligibility table that a linked Checking account have had a deposit, withdrawal, payment or transfer in the previous calendar month. The two statements of eligibility cannot both govern the monthly adjustment.

This clause prescribes a rate for "[n]on-personal TD Relationship Savings accounts", although the instrument is the Personal Deposit Account Agreement and Part II covers "ALL personal deposit Accounts". Whether non-personal accounts are governed by this Agreement at all is a question raised by reading the two together.

This clause permits linked-account information to be "made available to any other owner or signer on any of the accounts you have linked", but Part IV's "Disclosures of Account Information To Third Parties" states that the Bank will not disclose information about you or your Account except in nine enumerated cases, which do not include owners of linked accounts. The two disclosure rules conflict.

The account qualifies only if it "meets all of the following criteria", and criterion (a) is "[w]hether or not your TD Growth Money Market account qualifies" — the conclusion stated as one of its own conditions. That circularity leaves the qualification test indeterminate.

A qualifying transfer is "a recurring transfer of any amount from a TD Bank account", but "recurring" is not defined and no frequency or number of occurrences is stated. Whether a transfer set up to repeat but occurring once in the cycle qualifies cannot be determined.

This clause makes a single "Immediate transfer completed through Online Banking" qualify, although the preceding subparagraph defines a qualifying transfer as "a recurring transfer". The two definitions of what counts as a qualifying transfer cannot both stand as written.

The qualifying window runs from "the first business day" to "the last business day" of the statement cycle in lower case, while the Agreement defines "Business Day" as a capitalized term and the parallel TD Simple Savings clause uses an entirely different window. Whether the defined term is meant, and against which cycle, is left open.

Qualification is determined "[o]n the last business day of your statement cycle", yet the preceding clause permits a qualifying transfer to post on that same last business day. Whether a transfer posting on the determination day counts cannot be resolved from the two together.

This clause fixes a rate for "[n]on-personal TD Growth Money Market accounts" although this is the Personal Deposit Account Agreement and Part II §1 defines the covered Accounts as personal deposit Accounts. Whether the Agreement reaches non-personal accounts is unresolved.

Making linked-account information "available to any other owner or signer on any of the accounts you have linked" cannot be squared with Part IV's "Disclosures of Account Information To Third Parties", which limits disclosure to nine enumerated circumstances. Linked-account owners are not among them.

The rate and APY "are fixed for the term of the certificate and may only be changed at maturity", while the Amendments clause reserves the right to "change the terms of this Agreement or change the terms of your Account at any time". Whether the Bank may alter a CD rate mid-term is a direct clash between the two.

The tier rate is stated to be "paid on the full balance in the Account", whereas the "To Obtain the Annual Percentage Yield Disclosed" clause requires the minimum tier balance to be maintained "each day" to obtain that tier's APY. The interaction of the two determines what a customer whose balance dips below a tier is paid.

The clause directs the reader to "[t]he Chart on page 31", but the Health Savings Account balance tier structure it refers to is printed on page 30 immediately below. The cross-reference is simply wrong on its face.

This clause provides that "[i]n no circumstances can the amount withdrawn bring the balance to below the Minimum to Open", yet the Step Rate CD clause permits "[p]artial and full withdrawals ... without penalty" during each anniversary grace period and the maturity clause permits withdrawal of the funds. A full withdrawal cannot both be permitted and be barred by the Minimum to Open floor.

The "ten (10) day grace period" is stated in days that are neither Business Days nor Calendar Days as those terms are defined, while the parallel maturity grace period is expressed in Calendar Days. Which measure applies to a Step Rate CD anniversary withdrawal is not stated.

The No Catch CD is given one penalty-free principal withdrawal and "[m]ore than one withdrawal ... may result in a penalty", while the early withdrawal penalty table expressly covers "Basic, No Catch and IRA Add-Vantage CDs" with mandatory penalties. Whether and at what rate a second withdrawal is penalised cannot be answered from the two together.

Automatic renewal applies "[u]nless otherwise noted", without saying where such a note may appear or what form it must take. The qualifier leaves the renewal rule defeasible by an unidentified document.

On early closure, "[a]ccrued interest in an amount under $10 will not be paid except at the discretion of the Bank", forfeiting interest already accrued to the customer with no standard governing the discretion. Whether accrued interest can be withheld in this way is the construction question.

The fee is avoided by maintaining "the minimum required daily balance specified for your type of Account for that particular monthly cycle", which does not say whether the balance must be met on every day of the cycle or on average. "Minimum required daily balance" is the term to construe.

"There must have been at least one qualifying transfer" states no period, and the timing appears only two subparagraphs later in a differently expressed window. Read alone, the criterion has no time boundary at all.

A qualifying transfer is defined as "a recurring transfer of at least $25", but the very next subparagraph makes a one-off "Immediate transfer completed through Online Banking" qualify with no stated amount. The two definitions of a qualifying transfer conflict.

This clause qualifies an "Immediate transfer" that is neither recurring nor subject to the $25 minimum imposed by the preceding subparagraph's definition of a qualifying transfer. Whether the $25 floor applies to an Immediate transfer is unresolved between them.

The eligibility window runs "from the last business day of your previous service charge cycle" to "the second-to-last business day of your current service charge cycle", using lower-case business days and a window different from the one used for the TD Growth Money Market. Which days count, and whether a transfer counts for two consecutive cycles, is not stated.

This clause invites the customer to "stop receiving printed and mailed statements and switch to online statements only", yet the Periodic Statement clauses run the customer's reporting deadlines from "the statement mailing date" and deem statements available as of that date. For an online-only customer there is no mailing date, so the two provisions cannot be applied together.
Interest "begins to accrue no later than the Business Day we receive credit for the deposit", which fixes an outer limit but no actual accrual date. When accrual in fact begins is left to the Bank.

This clause promises notice "at least thirty (30) days in advance of any changes to these fees", while the Amendments clause reserves the right to change terms at any time on "such notice ... as we determine is appropriate". Which notice governs a fee increase cannot be settled from either clause alone.

The bonus is "limited to one bonus per Customer", using a capitalized "Customer" that the Agreement never defines, and the promotion exists only "[i]f we are offering such a promotion". Whether joint owners are one Customer, and whether any enforceable promise exists absent an announced promotion, are both open.

This Gift Card promotion says it "cannot be combined with any other offer", as do the cash-bonus and Direct Deposit-bonus promotions in the same section, though a single qualifying account opening could satisfy all three. Which offer a customer receives when more than one is running is not resolved between them.

The bonus requires the customer to "enroll in Direct Deposit on the spot during the promotional period", a phrase with no defined content — what enrolment consists of and how immediate it must be. "On the spot" is the term to construe.

Eligibility turns on depositing "money not already on deposit at TD Bank" and "new to bank money", neither of which is defined or tied to any lookback period. Whether funds recently withdrawn from a TD Bank account qualify cannot be determined.

Automatic renewal at the non-promotional rate applies "unless we notify you otherwise", with no period, method or content specified for that notice. The escape from the stated renewal rule is entirely at the Bank's option.

"A TD Bank personal checking account is required" does not say by when it must exist, whether it must remain open, or whether the CD owner must be an owner of it. The condition's content is indeterminate.

Renewal at the non-promotional rate applies "unless we notify you otherwise", with no notice period or method fixed. The customer cannot tell what renewal rate governs until the Bank chooses to speak.

The Policy declares that withdrawal rights "will be determined according to this policy", yet the Deposit Policy in Part I states that "[t]he Funds Availability Policy does not apply to items we have accepted for collection only" and the set-off and legal-process clauses permit holds outside it. The Policy's claim to govern availability is qualified elsewhere in ways it does not acknowledge.

The Policy applies "to all transaction accounts such as Checking and Interest Bearing Checking Accounts, and to Money Market, Savings, and Time Accounts", the "such as" leaving the class of covered transaction accounts open-ended. Which accounts are within the Policy is not fixed by the text.

This states a "general policy" of availability by the first Business Day after deposit, while the "Longer Delays May Apply" clauses permit availability on the second Business Day for unspecified check types and as late as the seventh for enumerated circumstances. Whether the first-Business-Day rule is a promise or merely a default the Bank may displace is the question.

"[T]he earliest time that we stop accepting deposits in our Stores for same-day credit is 8pm" fixes only a floor, so the actual cutoff at any given Store is unknowable, and the sentence runs on without punctuation after "8pm". The customer cannot determine the day of his deposit from this text.

Funds placed in a night depository are "considered deposited on the next Business Day the Bank or Store lockbox is open", while Part VI provides that items delivered by a Carrier are "considered deposited only when actually received by us and verified and credited to your account" and allows two Business Days to count the bag. The two rules for dating a night-depository deposit cannot both apply.

Funds deposited at non-proprietary ATMs "may not be available until the fifth (5th) Business Day", which states a possibility rather than a rule and gives no criterion for when the delay is imposed. "May not be available" is the phrase to construe.

This clause promises same-day availability for the listed deposits, but the "Longer Delays May Apply" clause allows the Bank to withhold funds "in some cases" and for enumerated circumstances without excepting the same-day categories. Whether the same-day list survives the longer-delay exceptions is unresolved.

"Depending on the type of check you deposit, funds may not be available until the second (2nd) Business Day" never identifies which types of check are subject to the delay. The trigger for the delay is left entirely unstated.

The extended-delay grounds include that "you have overdrawn your Account repeatedly, or would have overdrawn your account if checks had been honored in the last six (6) months", with no content given to "repeatedly", and the concluding promise is hedged to funds "generally" available by the seventh Business Day. Both terms leave the maximum hold indeterminate.

The new-account rules "may apply during the first thirty (30) days your account is open", so it is not stated whether or when they in fact apply, and "new Customer" is undefined. Whether a customer who already holds another account is a "new Customer" is also left open.

For new accounts "funds from all other check deposits will be available no later than the seventh (7th) Business Day", omitting the $200-by-the-first-Business-Day floor that the general "Longer Delays" clauses guarantee. Whether that floor survives for new customers cannot be answered from either clause alone.

These "additional special rules" run "during the first ninety (90) days your account is open", whereas the Special Rules For New Accounts they supplement run only for the first thirty days. Which schedule governs an ATM deposit made on, say, day sixty is unresolved between the two.

For new Customers, "[c]ash deposits ... made at a TD Bank ATM will be available ... on the first (1st) business day after the day of your deposit", while the Same Day Availability clause and the new-account in-Store rule make cash deposits available the same day. The two treatments of a new customer's cash deposit conflict.

This makes non-proprietary ATM check deposits unavailable until the seventh business day, while the general "Determining availability — ATM deposits" clause states that funds from any deposits at ATMs the Bank does not own "may not be available until the fifth (5th) Business Day". The two outer limits for the same deposit differ.

The clause permits a hold on funds in a different Account whenever the Bank cashes or accepts a check drawn on another bank, without tying that hold to any of the enumerated circumstances that justify longer delays elsewhere in the Policy. How this open-ended cross-account hold coexists with the Policy's availability schedules is the question.

This clause states that funds on collection items "are generally available within thirty (30) Calendar Days", although the Part I Deposit Policy provides that "[t]he Funds Availability Policy does not apply to items we have accepted for collection only" and that no credit is given until final credit is received. The two cannot both govern a foreign check sent for collection.

This clause allows the Bank to "charge you for the overdraft" on a returned item, while the Part I Deposit Policy already imposes a returned-item fee plus overdraft fees on reversal of the same provisional credit. Whether one charge or several are authorised for one returned item is unresolved between them.

The customer is "responsible for any losses" from non-conforming endorsements that the Bank may nonetheless accept, without any limit or causal link to the non-conformity. "Any losses" is the open-ended term a court would have to construe.

The disclosure describes the transfers "we are capable of handling" and then warns that "[s]ome of these may not apply to your Account", without saying which apply to which account type. Which EFT rights a given customer actually has cannot be determined from the Part.
Card use "may be restricted in certain countries due to security risks", identifying neither the countries nor the restrictions nor any notice. The scope of the reserved restriction is entirely open.

The card "may be cancelled after 13 months of inactivity" with no notice requirement, while the EFT Termination clause provides that "[t]he Bank may terminate the Electronic Funds Transfer Agreement by notifying you in writing". Whether cancelling the card for inactivity requires that written notice is unresolved between the two.

Direct deposits may be accepted into "your Checking, Savings or Money Market Deposit Accounts", whereas the neighbouring Pre-authorized Withdrawals and Telephone Transfers clauses limit the same services to "Statement Savings or Statement Money Market Deposit Accounts". Whether passbook and non-statement savings accounts are included differs between the clauses.

A converted check "is treated as an EFT and is not a negotiable instrument in its own right", carrying EFT error and unauthorized-transfer protections, while the Part I Pre-authorized Drafts clause deems any debit initiated by a party to whom you gave Account information "authorized by you". The same point-of-purchase debit falls under two inconsistent regimes.

The list of ATM capabilities is qualified by "Note: Some of these services may not be available at all terminals", without identifying which or where. The promise of ATM access is thereby left indeterminate.

"If a merchant receives authorization for a purchase, TD Bank cannot return that transaction unpaid even if your account is not in good standing", yet the Processing Order and Overdrafts clauses treat items that overdraw the Account as fee-generating and describe overdrafts as advances made "at our sole discretion". Whether a fee can be charged for a transaction the Bank concedes it had no power to refuse is the question raised by reading them together.

These are "[t]he standard daily limits (per card)", the word "standard" implying that other limits may be applied without saying when or how. What limit binds a particular customer is not fixed by the text.

The customer agrees not to make the PIN available "to anyone not authorized to sign on your Account", which by implication permits sharing it with authorized signers. How transfers made by a person given the PIN are treated under the Unauthorized Transfers clause is left unclear by that carve-out.

The customer may terminate "by calling us and subsequently providing written notice", without saying when termination takes effect or what happens between the call and the writing. The two-step requirement leaves the effective date of termination undetermined.

"For certain account types we will waive the fee for some non-TD ATM transactions as disclosed on the Personal Fee Schedule" identifies neither the account types nor the transactions, deferring both to a document that may change. "Certain" and "some" carry the whole waiver.

Reimbursement of third-party surcharges is promised only "[f]or some Checking Account types", with the qualifying types left to the Personal Fee Schedule. Which customers have the benefit cannot be told from the clause.

The refund depends on bringing in an ATM receipt "within 90 calendar days" in lower case, and applies only to "Accounts that Qualify for Surcharge Refunds", a category identified nowhere in the Agreement. Both the period and the qualifying accounts are indeterminate.

The exchange rate is "a rate selected by Visa from the range of rates available in wholesale markets ... which may vary from the rate Visa itself receives, or the government-mandated rate in effect", a disjunction that does not say which rate governs a given transaction. The customer cannot determine the applicable rate from the clause.

This promises a monthly statement where "the only possible transfers to or from your Account are direct deposits", while the Periodic Statements clause promises monthly statements "unless there are no checks written or no electronic transfers" and the Part I statement clause excuses statements altogether for inactive Accounts. The three statement obligations cannot all be applied to the same Account.

The monthly statement obligation is excused "unless there are no checks written or no electronic transfers in a particular month", so on its literal terms the absence of either category alone defeats the promise, though the sense requires "and". The disjunctive "or" is a mechanical defect that changes the meaning of the obligation.

The notice obligation for varying payments is placed on "the person (or organization) you are going to pay", a third party who is not a party to this Agreement, and the customer's alternative election has no mechanism for being communicated. Who owes the customer the ten-day notice is left unresolved.

A stop payment request must "precisely identify the account number, date and amount of the payment", yet the Notice of Varying Amounts clause immediately above contemplates pre-authorized payments whose amounts vary and are not known in advance. The precision requirement cannot be met for the very transfers this section covers.

"[Y]ou cannot place stop payments for purchases made by telephone, on the Internet, or with your Visa Debit Card" cannot be squared with the preceding clause's statement that "[p]re-authorized transfers from your Account(s) can be discontinued", since a recurring pre-authorized payment may be charged to the Visa Debit Card. Which rule governs a recurring debit-card payment is unresolved.

This clause makes the Bank "liable for your losses or damages" for failing to stop a timely-ordered pre-authorized transfer, while the Limited Liability clause bars liability absent bad faith and caps recovery at three months' fees and charges. The two liability rules cannot both govern the same failure.

This states that "[u]nless otherwise provided in the Agreement, you may not stop payment of electronic fund transfers", while the Right to Stop Payment clause in the same Part expressly permits pre-authorized transfers to be discontinued. Whether the Agreement "otherwise provides" is left to the reader to work out.

Framed as a safety tip, "[t]he activity of the ATM facility is being recorded by a surveillance camera or cameras" is a statement of present fact about every ATM facility, without qualification. Whether it is a representation the Bank must make good is the construction question.

Ten specific exceptions to the Bank's liability are introduced by "for instance" and closed by "There may be other exceptions stated in our Agreement with you", so the enumerated list neither limits nor identifies the exceptions. Whether the list is exhaustive is exactly what a court would be asked to decide.

The privacy promise is qualified by exceptions for "certain routine disclosures necessary for the completion of a transfer", disclosure "to certain third parties with whom we have joint marketing agreements" and "to our affiliates as permitted by law", none of which is bounded. The exceptions are broad enough to consume the undertaking not to disclose.
Notice must be given "within three (3) days" of discovery, using neither of the Agreement's two defined day conventions. Whether Business Days or Calendar Days are meant is not stated.

The clause says the customer "will not be liable for unauthorized purchases made with your Debit Card when used as if it were a Visa Credit Card" but then says he "can be held liable for fraudulent use of your Card and/or PIN when PIN-based transactions are made", without defining which transactions fall on which side. The $50/$500 tiers turn on that undefined distinction.

This gives the customer sixty Calendar Days after the statement was mailed to report transfers he did not make, while the Part I statement clause bars any claim about a matter shown on a statement unless reported within thirty Calendar Days of mailing. The two deadlines for the same statement entry are irreconcilable.

The Bank "must hear from you no later than sixty (60) Calendar Days after we sent you the FIRST statement on which the problem or error appeared", whereas the Part I Periodic Statement clause bars claims not reported within thirty Calendar Days of mailing. For an electronic transfer appearing on a statement the two notice periods conflict.

"[W]e may not provisionally credit your Account" if a written complaint is not received within ten Business Days, leaving it uncertain whether the failure forfeits provisional credit or merely permits the Bank to withhold it, and whether it affects the underlying claim. "May not" is the phrase carrying the consequence.

After setting out a forty-five day and a ninety day extended investigation period, the clause says "[i]f we decide to do this, we will credit your Account", without identifying which of the two extensions triggers the provisional credit obligation. The antecedent of "this" determines when the customer gets his money.

The substitute-check refund procedure entitles the customer to his loss up to the amount of the check plus interest, while the Limited Liability clause caps any recovery from the Bank at three months' fees and charges and bars liability absent bad faith. Whether the cap applies to a substitute check refund claim is unresolved between them.

A substitute check claim may be made "within 40 Calendar Days" of the mailing of the check or the statement, whichever is later, while the Part I Periodic Statement clause forbids asserting any claim about a matter shown on a statement unless notice was given within thirty Calendar Days of mailing. The two limitation periods for the same debit cannot both stand.

Part VI uses "this Agreement" to mean the Night Depository Agreement alone and redefines "you" as "the Depositor", although the same phrase and pronouns are defined for the whole instrument at the front. Every later reference in Part VI to "this Agreement" is therefore ambiguous as between the two documents.

The obligation falls on "all new Depositors", a capitalized term never defined and distinguished from the "Existing Depositors" of the next subparagraph only by the September 1, 2011 date. Who is a new as opposed to an existing Depositor is not stated.

"Existing Depositors" may keep using their own containers, while the preceding subparagraph requires "all new Depositors" to use Bank-supplied disposable bags; neither term is defined and the classes are not exhaustive. A depositor who resumes the service after a gap falls into neither category.

The clause deems the Carrier "your exclusive agent when items are in transit" even where, by its own first sentence, "[w]e may arrange for and pay for a Carrier to collect deposits from you". Whether a carrier selected, engaged and paid by the Bank can be the customer's exclusive agent is the question the clause creates.

Liability here is excluded except for loss "directly caused by our negligence or willful misconduct", while the Part I Limited Liability clause excludes all liability "unless we have acted in bad faith" and caps damages at three months' fees. The Agreement thus states two different standards of care for the same Bank.

"[T]he determination of our employee is conclusive as to the contents of the bags" makes the Bank the final judge of the amount deposited, while the next clause promises "ordinary care and ... reasonable commercial standards" in processing the bags. A conclusive determination leaves no room to test whether that care was exercised.

This allows "up to two Business Days following the day the bag is received" to count and credit the deposit, while the Funds Availability Policy provides that funds deposited in a night depository are considered deposited on the next Business Day the Bank is open and available on that schedule. The two dating and crediting rules conflict, and this clause also says the Policy "applies to all deposits".

The undertaking to "use ordinary care and adhere to the reasonable commercial standards of the banking business" sits against the preceding clause making the Bank employee's count "conclusive as to the contents of the bags" and the Liability of Bank clause disclaiming responsibility for loss "resulting from any cause whatsoever". Whether the ordinary care promise is enforceable at all depends on reading the three together.

Fees may be changed "in the manner specified in the Deposit Account Agreement", but that Agreement contains two different change-notice rules — the Amendments clause's notice "as we determine is appropriate" and Part II §7's thirty days' advance notice of fee changes. The cross-reference does not identify which manner is meant.

This declares the Night Depository Agreement "the entire agreement between you and us with respect to the use of the night depository service", while the introduction to the instrument states that "[t]his Agreement consists of Parts I-VI" together with the Rate Sheets, Fee Schedules and grids. Whether Part VI stands alone or is one part of a single integrated contract is unresolved.

Part VI controls over "any provision of the Deposit Account Agreement relative to the night depository service", but no criterion is given for when a general provision — the Limited Liability clause, the Funds Availability Policy, the Amendments clause — is "relative to" that service. The reach of the priority rule is what would be construed.

Part VI is governed by "the state laws that apply to your primary deposit account", a term used nowhere else and undefined, whereas the Part I Governing Law clause looks to the jurisdiction of the Store where the Account was opened. Which law governs, and which account is "primary" for a customer with several, is not answerable from the text.
